newsitem.title: FRANCE: France restarting botched Thomson group sale.
newsitem.headline: France restarting botched Thomson group sale.

text.p: Just a week after a botched first attempt, the French government has changed tack fast and decided to privatise state-owned defence and consumer electronics group Thomson SA in two parts, starting with defence arm Thomson-CSF.

The finance ministry announced the new strategy on Wednesday night in a brief statement, saying it now hoped to sell off the profitable defence business in early 1997 but would inject money into loss-making Thomson Multimedia before privatising it later.

It said the precise sale procedure would be decided "in the coming days" but the government would ensure the conditions for staff to become shareholders, raising the prospect of a sale by issuing shares rather than a direct company-to-company sell-off.

The suspension of the previous sale provoked widepread media accusations of government incompetence and demands by the South Korean government for an explanation after objection to the sale of Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo Electronics.

"The government ends the current procedure on Thomson SA and has decided to launch, under two separate procedures, the privatisation of Thomson-CSF, then Thomson Multimedia, openly and respecting the state's patrimonial interests," it said.
"Thomson-CSF will be privatised as soon as possible in the early months of 1997," it said, adding that the state will keep a golden share in the company to protect France's defence interests.

The government announced on December 4 that it had suspended a plan to sell Thomson SA in its entirety for one symbolic franc to French missiles-to-publishing firm Lagardere Groupe and South Korea's Daewoo Electronics.

The plan ran into trouble when the independent Privatisation Commission objected to the plan for Lagardere to sell on Thomson Multimedia, one of the world's biggest television set and video player makers, to Daewoo, again for a single symbolic franc.

It was not clear after the finance ministry statement on the new strategy whether Lagardere, Daewoo or another bidder which had been sidelined by the government originally, France's Alcatel Alsthom, would be in the running again.
None of the French firms concerned nor the finance ministry was available for comment after the late-night statement.
Thomson SA owns 58 percent of Thomson-CSF and all of Thomson Multimedia, which has been promised a state recapitalisation of at least 11 billion francs ($2 billion).

"As far as Thomson Multimedia is concerned, the government confirms that the company, which has to implement a recovery plan, will be recapitalised before privatisation," the finance ministry's statement said.
The Privatisation Commission challenged the sale of Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo on the grounds that promises on employment and investment from the South Korean were not binding.
The sale also amounted to the state hiving off a firm whose "first-rate resources" in digital technology had been developed with state cash, from which the buyer would benefit.
The decision was read differently by Seoul, which demanded an explanation, and Daewoo, where a top executive described it as "subjective, unfair and even discriminatory".
At the end of 1995, Thomson Multimedia had debts of 13.8 billion francs ($2.65 billion) and Thomson-CSF debts of 2.3 billion francs ($440 million).

The Thomson Multimedia sale to Daewoo had provoked fierce controversy in France where thousands of employees marched in protest, worried for their future and infuriated even further by remarks from Prime Minister Alain Juppe that the company was worth nothing.
